# What is STEP? {#sec-introduction}

STEP is the common name for ISO 10303, *Industrial automation systems and integration -- Product data representation and exchange* [@iso10303-1].
The acronym stands for *Standard for the Exchange of Product model data*.
In everyday use "a STEP file" means a text file with the extension `.stp` or `.step` that holds a 3D model, usually a part or an assembly.

## The problem STEP solves

Every CAD system stores geometry in its own proprietary format.
When a design has to move between companies, tools, or decades, those formats become a liability.
STEP defines a neutral, vendor-independent representation so that a model written by one system can be read by another without loss of the information the standard covers.

STEP is not just a geometry format.
Depending on the application protocol in use, a file can also carry:

- product structure, such as assemblies and their component instances;
- product manufacturing information (PMI), such as tolerances and annotations;
- colours, layers, and presentation data;
- configuration and revision metadata.

## The standard in one paragraph

ISO 10303 is not one document but a family of several hundred parts.
A small number of them define the foundations: a data modelling language called EXPRESS [@iso10303-11], a text file format for exchanging data [@iso10303-21], and a set of shared resource schemas that describe geometry, topology, and product structure.
On top of those foundations, *Application Protocols* (APs) select and constrain the resources for a particular industry need.
The AP you will meet most often today is AP 242, *Managed model-based 3D engineering* [@iso10303-242], which superseded the older AP 203 and AP 214.

## Parts of ISO 10303 you will meet in this book

| Part | Name | Role |
|-----:|------|------|
| 1 | Overview and fundamental principles | Vocabulary and architecture of the whole standard |
| 11 | EXPRESS language reference manual | The schema language every other part is written in |
| 21 | Clear text encoding of the exchange structure | The `.stp` text file format |
| 41–4x | Integrated generic resources | Shared schemas for geometry, topology, product structure, and more |
| 203 / 214 / 242 | Application protocols | Which entities may appear in a file, and how they fit together |

The rest of this book walks through these layers from the bottom up, starting with the file you can open in a text editor.
